title: The Spirit Garden
description:
The Spirit Garden is a 20,000 plus square foot Indigenous cultural space at Nathan Phillips Square that invites learning, remembrance, and ceremony. Its elements include a Teaching Lodge with glulam structure, a reflecting pool, a Two Row Wampum walkway, sculptural artworks, and crafted metal that carries stories as well as structure. The site has been recognized for precision and craft, which reflects the care required to bring the design to life. 
 
 Mariani Metal served as sheet metal and specialty metal fabricator for the project. Our team translated the design intent for brass and copper alloy cladding into buildable assemblies that maintain crisp edges, consistent seams, and even reflectivity in open sun. We coordinated panel geometry around complex transitions at the Teaching Lodge and landscape thresholds, verified tolerances with shop mockups, and refined clip systems that allow thermal movement without read through on the surface. Stainless fabrications were detailed for durability and for maintenance access so inscriptions, artwork interfaces, and water features remain sharp over time. The finished metalwork supports the cultural narrative of the place while withstanding heavy daily use in the city’s most public square.
architect: Gow Hastings Architects with Two Row Architect

title: Glen Road Pedestrian Bridge
description:
Spanning the Rosedale Valley Ravine, the rebuilt Glen Road pedestrian bridge and companion tunnel reconnect Rosedale with North St. James Town. The new three-span steel-girder bridge with inclined legs carries a 4.8-metre-wide multi-use path; the tunnel beneath Bloor Street East was widened to improve openness, sightlines, and accessibility. The crossing and tunnel reopened to the public in late May–early June 2025. 
 
 Mariani Metal delivered precision architectural metalwork aligned with the bridge’s contemporary barrier concept, coordinating closely with the design and site teams to develop shop details, full-scale fit-ups, and installation sequencing that protected active public areas. Tight-tolerance fabrication and verified connections ensured clean sightlines, durable interfaces with concrete and steel, and a refined finish appropriate to a high-use civic structure.

title: vivaNext BRT Stations
description:
The vivaNext program defines a family of rapid transit stations that are light, legible, and consistent across the corridor. Canopies appear thin and continuous, structural glass is clear and true, and components repeat without visual drift from site to site. This clarity depends on fabricated parts that are dimensionally disciplined and finishes that hold up to daily use, weather, and maintenance cycles. 
 
 Mariani Metal was responsible for engineering and fabricating key structural elements that made Gehry’s vision possible. The vast canopy of the Galleria Italia required a precise lattice of steel framing, fabricated to exacting tolerances to support the delicate balance of glass and wood. Inside the gallery, Mariani also constructed and installed the dramatic spiral staircases that rise through Walker Court. These elements demanded complex welding, trial assemblies, and careful sequencing to achieve seamless integration within a historic building. 
 
 Mariani Metal fabricated and installed architectural steel and metal cladding for select stations within the program. Working from standardized intent, we developed production ready models that protected the station language while making the parts economical to repeat. Canopy ribs, purlins, edge trims, and cladding were fabricated with fixture control so weld profiles and gap lines match from one station to the next. Hidden fasteners and drip edges keep the silhouette clean and direct water away from glass and passenger zones. Coating systems were selected and applied to transit durability criteria, with field touch up methods defined in advance to keep stations looking new after installation and during maintenance. The stations read as a single family along the route, and the metalwork helps that identity stay consistent regardless of site, contractor, or phase.
contractor: Various, including joint ventures across program phases

title: Le Jardin sur Madison
description:
Le Jardin is conceived as a hospitality-forward destination where calm proportion, clear circulation, and carefully edited materials create a sense of ease. The exterior reads as a series of clean horizontal lines that frame arrivals and terraces. Inside, guests move through light, uncluttered spaces where metal, glass, and stone meet with quiet precision. The identity of the venue relies on details that look simple yet perform under real traffic conditions and seasonal change. 
 
Mariani Metal delivered the architectural metalwork that anchors this visual clarity. Our team partnered in a design-assist capacity to refine interfaces between metal, glazing, millwork, and stone, and to confirm tolerances before the first piece was cut. Entrance portals, canopy frames, guards, and trim were modeled for fit and movement, then fabricated as shop-finished assemblies to control quality and finish consistency. We used laser-cut plate and formed sections to keep sightlines thin, continuous TIG finishing to eliminate visible seams, and concealed fasteners so the architecture stays quiet to the eye. Installation sequencing protected finished surfaces while allowing the venue to maintain an active construction schedule. The result is a durable, premium environment where the metalwork holds the lines of the architecture and invites close viewing without calling attention to itself.

title: 7 Dale Condominium
description:
7 Dale sits at the edge of the Rosedale Valley and balances contemporary living with a careful reading of context. The architecture pairs masonry and stone with glass and warm metal accents, creating a composition that feels crafted rather than loud. Every balcony line, screen, and guard has to respect the weight and texture of the heritage fabric while meeting modern codes for wind, loading, and safety. 
 
 Mariani Metal engineered and fabricated the custom exterior metalwork that gives the building its refined edges. Balcony guards and feature screens were designed to sit lightly against stone and brick, with anchorage that respects existing substrates and allows alignment adjustments without overloading the heritage structure. Fabrication emphasized clean corners, true planes, and consistent patina so that the metal reads as one family from street to penthouse. Coordination with curtain wall and stone trades set the joint logic and movement breaks, which keeps lines straight through seasonal change and long term service. Installation was phased for a tight urban site, with hoist friendly modules and protected finishes that could go in late without disrupting adjacent work. The result is a quietly confident façade where metal, stone, and glass support each other and where the detailing rewards close inspection.
contractor: Platinum Vista and project GC per phase

title: Garrison Crossing
description:
Also known as Garrison Crossing, the project delivers two multi span stainless steel bridges that connect Stanley Park to Fort York across active rail corridors. The design is slender and highly visible, which makes fabrication accuracy and finish control critical at every stage from shop to lift. 
 
 Mariani Metal was the steel fabricator for the bridges. We produced Duplex stainless steel arch and deck assemblies using fixtures that hold camber and geometry through welding and handling. Panel seams, rib spacing, and connection details were coordinated so that repetition produces visual consistency from one span to the next. Shop coatings and on site protection plans were tuned for stainless performance and construction logistics. The north span was lifted in a single piece using a heavy crawler crane to avoid rail closures, which required precise rigging points and a verified center of gravity. The completed bridges give Toronto a resilient, low maintenance connection with a finish that will remain bright for decades.

title: The Well
description:
At The Well, a sweeping 7.7-acre mixed-use precinct in downtown Toronto featuring seven interconnected buildings, a three-storey glass-and-steel canopy, and a vibrant pedestrian spine, the development redefines city life by integrating office, retail, and residential programs into a cohesive urban ecosystem. 
 
 Mariani Metal fabricated and installed precision architectural-metal assemblies for the pedestrian spine’s built environment. Working closely with the design and façade teams, we selected premium stainless and architectural alloy finishes to deliver long-term performance in a heavily trafficked, publicly accessible zone. Full-scale mockups verified alignment, drainage integration, and connection geometry ahead of site delivery, ensuring seamless installation while the precinct remained operational. The outcome is a seamless urban corridor where sculptural precision meets enduring engineering, a testament to Mariani’s commitment to excellence in architectural metalwork for defining projects.
contractor: EllisDon Construction Services Inc. for the joint venture of RioCan REIT & Allied Properties REIT

title: TD Terrace
description:
At TD Terrace, a striking 48-storey steel-composite tower sculpted to respond to site conditions and wind loads, the building sets a new benchmark for workplace architecture in Toronto’s financial core. 
 
 Mariani Metal was engaged to deliver precision architectural metalwork for the tower’s signature façade and public-realm metal elements. Working closely with the design and façade teams, we curated premium stainless steel and architectural alloy finishes, developed full-scale mock-ups to validate complex joint geometry and edge detailing, and coordinated installation sequencing to maintain active zones during construction. The outcome is a dynamic, sculptural tower base and vertical profile that exemplify Mariani’s commitment to craftsmanship, durability, and refined architectural metalwork.
architect: Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture (Design) / B+H Architects (Architect of Record)

title: Four Seasons Downtown Staircase
description:
Four Seasons Hotel New York Downtown sits at the base of 30 Park Place, an 82-storey tower designed by Robert A.M. Stern Architects rising above Tribeca and the Financial District, one block from the World Trade Center. The hotel occupies the lower 24 floors with interiors by Yabu Pushelberg, whose work defines the benchmark for contemporary luxury hospitality design across North America and internationally. 
 
 The lobby staircase is the centrepiece of the arrival sequence: a sweeping elliptical form descending from the ballroom level to the ground floor lobby, with marble treads set within a continuous curved steel stringer structure and enclosed by a full-height lattice balustrade fabricated in a bronze-toned finish. The balustrade pattern is a rectangular Chinese fretwork, laser-cut across every panel and wrapped continuously around the full curve of the stair from base to upper landing without a single interruption in the geometry. Mariani Metal fabricated the complete staircase assembly, producing the curved stringer structure, the laser-cut lattice panels, and the continuous formed handrail that traces the ellipse from floor to floor. The lattice demanded precision cutting and panel-to-panel alignment so the fretwork pattern read as one unbroken field around a form that shifts in radius continuously. Every panel was unique in width as the curve tightened, and every joint between panels was resolved in fabrication so that nothing on site required correction. 
 
 Viewed from above, the staircase is a perfect composition of geometry, material, and craft. It is the kind of object that only gets made once, and only by a fabricator willing to hold that standard across every single piece.
location: 27 Barclay Street, New York City, New York

title: Little Island - Pier 55
description:
Little Island is a 2.4-acre public park and performance destination on the Hudson River, held above the water by 132 unique concrete piles, each topped with a tulip-shaped planter, that fuse together to create a richly planted undulating landscape accessible by boardwalk from Manhattan's Lower West Side. The park contains three outdoor performance spaces including an acoustically optimised 700-seat amphitheatre, a 200-seat spoken word stage, and a flexible central venue, woven through with planting across nearly 400 species of trees, shrubs, grasses, and perennials. The project, funded by Barry Diller and Diane von Furstenberg and eight years in the making, opened in 2021 as the most ambitious new piece of public infrastructure on the Manhattan waterfront in a generation. 
 
 Every edge of that undulating landscape required a railing. The park's rolling topography is traced by benches, railings, and meandering paths that follow the contour of the landscape from the gangplank entries to the uppermost viewing points at the park's north and northeast elevations. Mariani Metal fabricated the bronze railing system installed throughout the park, producing the handrail and balustrade assemblies that follow every path, overlook, stair, and performance terrace across the full 2.4 acres. A park of this topographic complexity generates railing geometry that is almost entirely non-repetitive: each run follows a different radius, pitch, and orientation as the landscape rises and falls, and the bronze finish needed to remain consistent in tone and texture across an outdoor installation exposed to salt air, sun, and the full range of a New York climate year-round. Fabrication required resolving every unique section in the shop before delivery, with field adjustments designed out of the process rather than left to be solved on site. 
 
 Bronze at this scale, in this setting, in front of this volume of daily visitors, has no margin for inconsistency. Mariani held that standard across the entire park.
location: Pier 55, Hudson River Park, New York City, New York
architect: Heatherwick Studio / MNLA (Mathews Nielsen Landscape Architects)

title: The Bow
description:
The Bow is one of the most structurally ambitious office towers ever built in Canada. Designed by Foster + Partners in collaboration with Zeidler Partnership Architects, the 58-storey crescent-shaped tower rises 236 metres above Calgary's downtown core and was, at its completion in 2012, the tallest building in the country outside of Toronto. Its defining feature is a triangular steel diagrid system applied to a curved building from a North American first, which minimizes structural steel tonnage while freeing up floor plate and maximising access to natural light and views of the Rocky Mountains. Three six-storey sky gardens punctuate the office floors, and a full-height atrium running the concave face of the tower acts as a thermal buffer zone across Calgary's extreme climate range. 
 
 Mariani Metal was engaged by Ledcor to deliver the architectural metalwork within the tower, contributing the precision fabrication that finishes a building of this calibre at the human scale. Working within one of the most technically complex construction programmes in Canadian history, Mariani coordinated closely with the construction schedule to deliver metalwork that met the exacting tolerances demanded by Foster + Partners' design intent. The building's geometry, with its continuously curving floor plates and exposed structural framing carried through all 58 floors, meant that every component had to be fabricated with consistency across a building section that shifts incrementally from base to crown. 
 
 The Bow received the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat Award for Best Tall Building in the Americas in 2013, the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction National Award, and the Calgary Mayor's Urban Design Award. It remains the standard against which commercial construction in Western Canada is measured.
architect: Foster + Partners (Design) / Zeidler Partnership Architects (Architect of Record)

title: Day's End
description:
Day's End is a permanent public art project commissioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art, located in Hudson River Park along the southern edge of Gansevoort Peninsula, directly across from the Museum. The work consists of an architectural outline of a pier made of stainless steel tubes and precast concrete, tracing the exact dimensions and location of the original Pier 52 shed that once stood on the site. Day's End measures 52 feet high at its peak, 65 feet wide, and 325 feet long, nearly the length of a football field. Seven years in the making, the $17 million sculpture is one of the largest permanent public art installations ever completed in the United States. 
 
 Hammons envisioned a slender frame comprising as few parts as possible, so the engineers at Guy Nordenson and Associates designed complex pipes capable of reliably bearing the weight of the colossal structure. Their thinness made them susceptible to wind vibration, requiring a special welding technique to fortify the structure's integrity throughout. The sculpture is made of high durability and corrosion-resistant super duplex stainless steel with a smooth finish designed to require little maintenance over time. 
 
 Mariani Metal completed the overall assembly of Day's End in Toronto, machining the top couplers and prefabricating the beams and columns into large sections so they could be connected on site with minimal construction time and reduced risk of environmental disturbance to the Hudson River. Working to Guy Nordenson and Associates' structural engineering programme, Mariani produced components where dimensional accuracy was absolute: the sculpture was required to occupy the precise coordinates of Matta-Clark's 1975 intervention, meaning every fabricated section had to land exactly where history demanded it. The groundbreaking took place in September 2019 and the sculpture was unveiled in May 2021. It stands permanently on the waterfront as one of the most consequential works of public art fabricated in Canada and installed in the United States in a generation.
location: Pier 52, Gansevoort Peninsula, Hudson River Park, New York City, New York

title: Art Gallery of Ontario
description:
Frank Gehry's CA$276 million transformation of the Art Gallery of Ontario was his first project on Canadian soil, and one of the most technically demanding renovations in the country's architectural history. The expansion added 97,000 square feet to one of North America's largest art museums, weaving new construction through building fabric that spanned four separate eras of the original structure. At the centre of that challenge was the staircase: a sculptural, enclosed spiral that cantilevers 11 metres beyond the rear facade of the building, linking Walker Court with the new Centre for Contemporary Art and overlooking Grange Park below. 
 
 Mariani Metal fabricated and assembled the staircase across 22 curved segments, each unique in geometry and all oversized, with the largest section measuring 14 by 15 feet. The project demanded exacting welding standards, with fabrication plans submitted to the Canadian Welding Bureau for quality assurance at every stage. Large sections were produced at Mariani's Etobicoke facility, then transported to Bolton for sandblasting and painting before being delivered to the site under permit and police escort. Installation required the components to be assembled in mid-air, with temporary supports holding each piece in position while the structure took its final form, a three-dimensional puzzle built to millimetre tolerances at cantilevered height. 
 
 The completed staircase is among the defining features of the Gehry renovation. It is the kind of work that rewards close inspection and announces itself from the street: curved, confident, and precisely made.

title: Rosaline Sharp Pavilion
description:
The Rosalie Sharp Pavilion sits at the southeast corner of Dundas and McCaul Streets, directly across from Frank Gehry's Art Gallery of Ontario, in one of the most architecturally charged intersections in Toronto. Commissioned by OCAD University, the project transformed an existing administrative office building into the university's Experiential Learning Centre, with Bortolotto's design wrapping the modest 2.5-storey structure in a perforated stainless steel facade scrim that functions simultaneously as solar shading, wayfinding, and civic statement. The scrim's laser-cut pattern encodes a data visualization map of Toronto's arts community, with circles denoting galleries, chevrons marking artist clusters, and the density of perforations shifting as the map moves outward from OCAD at its centre. 
 
 Mariani Metal fabricated the full front facade assembly, producing the stainless steel panels and the structural sub-frame that holds them proud of the building's insulated envelope. The geometry of the scrim required panels to curve and peel away at the outer edges, demanding precise forming and consistent surface quality across every sheet so the pattern read as a unified field from street level. Structural steel outriggers were fabricated to hold the scrim off the face of the building at a controlled depth, creating shadow and layered texture throughout the day as light conditions change. Tolerances were held tightly across the full facade height to ensure the perforated pattern aligned and the edges curled cleanly without distortion. 
 
 The completed pavilion has been published in Azure Magazine, Canadian Architect, and The Architect's Newspaper, and recognized with an Architecture Masterprize. It is a project where material precision and conceptual ambition are inseparable, and where the fabrication quality is visible to every person who passes that corner.

title: University of Toronto
description:
The University of Toronto's Landmark Project is one of the largest landscape infrastructure undertakings in Canadian academic history, transforming 17 acres of the historic St. George campus into a pedestrian-focused, accessible, and culturally significant precinct. Centred on King's College Circle, Hart House Circle, Sir Daniel Wilson Quad, and the Back Campus Fields, the project restructured the entire outdoor heart of the downtown campus, removing surface vehicles, installing an underground parkade beneath King's College Circle, and introducing one of the largest geo-exchange heating systems in the country. 
 
 Mariani Metal contributed fabrication across two distinct and technically different scopes within the broader project. On the north side of campus, Mariani fabricated the fascia and soffit cladding for the KPMB-designed parking pavilion structure, producing the metal envelope that wraps the above-grade garage access point adjacent to the Medical Sciences Building. The geometry required clean, consistent panel geometry at a human scale, with surfaces that would read as resolved and restrained within a heritage landscape context. On the south side, Mariani fabricated the bronze structural elements for Ziibiing, the Indigenous gathering landscape designed by Brook McIlroy's Indigenous Design Studio. The centrepiece of Ziibiing is the Knowledge House, an open-sided bronze pavilion supported by 13 columns symbolizing the 13 moons of the year, with a faceted carapace-like bronze soffit etched with star constellation patterns and a central aperture aligned to the North Star. Four branching sculptural bronze forms mark the cardinal directions across the site. 
 
 Fabricating the bronze elements demanded exacting control over patina, weld quality, and surface texture to honour the cultural and ceremonial significance of the structure they were producing. The Ziibiing landscape opened in September 2024 and has since been recognized by Canadian Architect as one of the most significant recent works of Indigenous design in the country.
architect: KPMB Architects (Fascia and Soffit Cladding) / Brook McIlroy Indigenous Design Studio (Ziibiing)

title: West Block - House of Commons Interim Chamber
description:
The rehabilitation of the West Block of Parliament is one of the largest heritage restoration projects ever undertaken in North America. The 19th-century building was completely modernised while its heritage and character-defining elements were preserved with precision and care. At the centre of the programme was a challenge with no Canadian precedent: the existing courtyard of the building needed to be converted into a fully functioning interim House of Commons Chamber, capable of seating 338 Members of Parliament, while Centre Block underwent its own decade-long rehabilitation. 
 
 The design response by EVOQ and Architecture49 was architecturally bold and historically respectful in equal measure. A series of tree-like steel columns, drawn directly from the neo-Gothic language of the original building, were devised to support a 51 by 55 metre curved glass roof spanning the full width of the courtyard. The roof system comprises approximately 1,400 diamond-shaped double-insulated glass panels and incorporates fixed and operable daylight control louvers concealed within a layered attic construction that functions as a thermal buffer across Ottawa's extreme seasonal range. 
 
 Mariani Metal fabricated the ornamental and architectural metalwork within the Chamber, producing components that had to meet the exacting standards of a federally designated heritage building while integrating seamlessly with a contemporary structural system of significant complexity. Working within the constraints of an active Parliamentary precinct, Mariani coordinated fabrication and delivery to a programme where sequencing and precision were non-negotiable. Every visible metal element was required to honour the Gothic Revival character of the surrounding stone fabric while holding the clean geometry demanded by the contemporary insertion above. 
 
 Construction commenced in January 2011 and was completed in November 2018, with the House of Commons sitting in the new Chamber from January 2019. The project stands as a benchmark for what heritage rehabilitation at national scale demands of every trade involved.

title: Axium Packaging
description:
Axium Packaging's new Brampton facility represents an $80 million investment and consolidates the company's Canadian manufacturing presence into a 227,000 square foot plant purpose-built for precision, efficiency, and long-term operation. The facility was designed to be LEED Silver compliant, placing sustainability requirements on every system and every finish within the building. Designed by Pearce McCluskey Architects and delivered by Leeswood Construction, the programme called for a building that could house advanced manufacturing operations while presenting a professional, well-resolved image appropriate to a global company establishing its flagship Canadian base. 
 
 Mariani Metal fabricated the architectural metalwork across the facility, delivering the structural and ornamental steel elements that define the building's interior and entry environments. In a manufacturing context, metal detailing carries particular weight: it is visible to clients, employees, and visitors daily, and it needs to perform without maintenance while reading as considered and permanent. Mariani's scope included canopy and entry metalwork, interior railings, and feature steelwork within the office and reception areas, with fabrication calibrated to the clean, industrial aesthetic that Pearce McCluskey's design called for. Every component was produced to tight dimensional tolerances and delivered to a construction schedule with no float, coordinating with Leeswood's programme to ensure sequenced installation that did not interfere with the parallel fit-out trades working across the large floor plate. 
 
 The completed facility opened in 2024 and positions Axium as one of the most capable sustainable packaging manufacturers in the Canadian market.

title: Welland Canal Fallen Workers Memorial
description:
The Welland Canal Fallen Workers Memorial, unveiled on November 12, 2017, honours the 137 men who lost their lives during the construction of the Welland Canal between 1913 and 1932. An engineering landmark linking Lake Erie and Lake Ontario, the canal was built by thousands of workers from 16 countries, many of them new to Canada, all of them part of a defining chapter in the nation's history. The memorial fulfills a promise made at the canal's opening in 1932, when a government minister called on the country to remember those who perished. It took 85 years to keep it. 
 
 Designed by Toronto's Dereck Revington Studio, the memorial is composed of four elements, The Gates of Remembrance, The Veil, The Timeline, and The Lock, each contributing to a landscape of reflection, memory, and civic reckoning. The steel components at the heart of the design demanded a fabricator capable of working to exacting tolerances, with surface finishes ranging from deep black to mirror-polished materials that carry both structural and symbolic weight. 
 
 Mariani Metal contributed architectural metalwork to the project, bringing the precision and finish quality the design required. Structural integrity and visual permanence both held to the same standard. Some projects are measured in square footage. This one is measured in names.

title: Garrison Point Staircase
description:
Garrison Point is a master-planned residential community at the edge of Liberty Village and Fort York, comprising two residential towers standing at 29 and 35 storeys over a shared podium, with 744 units, retail at grade, and a 3.9-acre public park at its centre. The project was designed by Hariri Pontarini Architects with interiors by Studio Munge, one of Canada's most awarded luxury interior design practices. Studio Munge's programme for the amenity levels set a hospitality standard that demanded the same material quality and precision detailing found in the five-star hotel projects for which the firm is internationally known. 
 
 Mariani Metal was engaged as both engineer and fabricator for the amenity staircase, a sculptural steel and glass assembly connecting the shared amenity floors within the podium. Serving as engineer on a residential staircase of this character requires more than structural competence: it requires an understanding of how a visible steel structure behaves across its full service life, how connections read at close range, and how fabrication decisions at the shop translate into finished form on site. Mariani carried that responsibility across both disciplines, producing engineering documentation and fabrication drawings in-house before building the staircase at the Etobicoke facility and coordinating installation with TMG's programme. The geometry was resolved to hold clean sight lines from multiple levels, with balustrade panels, handrail profiles, and stringer details all fabricated to the tolerances that Studio Munge's design intent required. 
 
 At a development where every finish decision was benchmarked against a luxury hospitality standard, the staircase needed to perform at the same level. It does.
location: Garrison Crossing, Ordnance Street, Toronto, Ontario

title: Ten York Condominium
description:
Ten York rises 65 storeys above the intersection of York and Harbour Streets, its triangular tower floor plan, inspired by the geometry of the wedge-shaped site, terminating in a sharp glass prow at its western end. Completed in 2019, the tower features gleaming glass cladding and platinum vertical fins that give Ten York the visual language of a precision-made object rather than a conventional residential high-rise. That standard of finish carried directly into the building's base. The four-storey entrance lobby was conceived as a gateway element connecting to One York across the street, framing the primary arrival point into Toronto's Southcore Office and Entertainment District. At that scale, the lobby is effectively a civic interior, and every material decision within it was held to the standard of the building's position on the waterfront skyline. 
 
 Mariani Metal fabricated the lobby columns, the defining vertical elements that structure the four-storey arrival space and set the material tone for everything a resident or visitor encounters upon entry. Columns at this scale in a lobby of this ambition are not background elements: they are the primary architectural objects of the room, and they need to be fabricated with the kind of precision that survives close, repeated, daily inspection across the full life of the building. Working in collaboration with Classic Crystal, Mariani produced the column assemblies to exacting profile and surface finish requirements, with geometry held consistently across each unit so that the columns read as a disciplined family from entry to ceiling. Connections, base details, and cap conditions were all resolved in fabrication before arriving on site, with installation sequenced to protect finished surfaces within Tridel's fit-out programme. 
 
 In a building where the quality of execution is visible in every detail, the lobby columns deliver exactly what Ten York's standard demands.

title: 50 Wellesley Tree
description:
50 Wellesley Station is a 37-storey residential tower by Plaza, designed by Quadrangle Architects at the northeast corner of Yonge and Wellesley Street, directly adjacent to the Wellesley subway station. The building sits within one of the most densely trafficked pedestrian intersections in downtown Toronto, and Quadrangle's design responded to that condition by anchoring the podium with a piece that functions simultaneously as architecture, public art, and identity marker. The main feature of the building is the podium and its copper tree-like sculpture, photographed from multiple angles and across different times of day, including its lighting at night. The branching canopy structure rises from the podium level, casting a sheltering presence over the street-level entrance and giving the building a singular identity within a neighbourhood dense with residential towers competing for attention. 
 
 Mariani Metal fabricated the tree canopy structure in collaboration with Classic Crystal, producing the branching copper assembly that defines the building's public face. A sculptural form of this nature presents fabrication challenges distinct from conventional architectural metalwork: the geometry is non-repetitive, each branch diverging at a unique angle from the primary trunk, and the copper finish needs to read as continuous and coherent across a structure that is inherently irregular. Mariani resolved the geometry in the fabrication shop, building each branching section to drawing tolerances before transporting and assembling the canopy on site in sequence with the podium construction programme. The copper patina was specified and controlled to ensure a consistent tone across the entire assembly, accounting for the variation in surface orientation and exposure that a three-dimensional branching form produces. 
 
 The completed tree canopy is the element that makes 50 Wellesley recognisable from the street before any signage is visible.

title: Weatherhead School of Management
description:
The Weatherhead School of Management at Case Western Reserve University stands as a striking example of architectural innovation, featuring Gehry's signature design of complex, flowing geometries. This project pushed the boundaries of architectural and engineering possibilities, with its sculptural, wave-like design that seems to emerge from the ground and cascade upwards. 
 
 Mariani Metal was entrusted with the fabrication of the building’s steel framework, which forms the skeleton beneath its gleaming stainless steel exterior. The design, brought to life through nearly 1,200 CATIA 3D models, required precise execution and extensive collaboration between the architect, contractor, and engineering teams. 
 
 The building's framework consists of 700 tons of pipe and structural steel, engineered to support the complex, curved shape of the exterior shell. Mariani Metal's role in this iconic project involved the fabrication of highly detailed structural elements, fabricated to exacting tolerances and assembled with precision. Each piece was custom-designed to ensure that it could integrate seamlessly with Gehry's ambitious vision. 
 
 Upon completion, the Weatherhead School of Management became a stunning addition to Cleveland’s architectural landscape. The use of stainless steel not only emphasizes the project's futuristic aesthetic but also contributes to its durability and visual impact, making the building a standout piece of modern architecture.

title: United States Air Force Memorial
description:
The United States Air Force Memorial stands as a powerful tribute to the service and values of the U.S. Air Force, symbolizing flight, spirit, and the core values of integrity, service, and excellence. Rising to a height of 270 feet, the memorial is a testament to architectural ambition and engineering precision, with a structure composed of 1 million lbs. of pure stainless steel. 
 
 Mariani Metal played a key role in bringing this monumental vision to life, contributing to the fabrication of the towering steel spires that define the memorial's shape. The project’s complex design required groundbreaking research and development, resulting in innovative methods for efficient fabrication and assembly. 
 
 Mariani’s team engineered a solution to lift and position the massive steel components, using nylon slings to raise sections weighing up to 40 feet high. This in-shop fabrication method allowed for unparalleled precision and efficiency, ensuring the structure’s success in both design and execution. 
 
 The completed memorial, with its stunningly curved stainless steel spires, not only captures the essence of flight but also stands as a monument to the dedication and excellence of the U.S. Air Force. Mariani’s contribution to this landmark project highlighted the company's capability to handle complex, high-profile projects that demand both innovation and precision.

title: The New York Times Building
description:
The New York Times Building, designed by Renzo Piano, is a striking fusion of form and function, with its translucent ceramic exterior and powerful structural design. Standing 52 stories tall, the building serves as a beacon of modern architecture, where art and engineering intersect seamlessly. The building’s façade, lined with ceramic beams, projects an elegant yet commanding presence, while the interior represents a space designed for creativity and innovation. 
 
 Mariani Metal was entrusted with providing the structural backbone for this iconic skyscraper. The project required an expert blend of strength and artistry, with Mariani’s team fabricating and installing the prominent supportive beams that define the building’s imposing physique. These beams, which highlight the strength of the structure, contrast beautifully with the delicate radiance of the ceramic exterior, balancing the bold and subtle elements of the design. 
 
 Mariani's meticulous attention to detail was evident throughout the fabrication process, ensuring that the materials not only supported the architectural vision but also contributed to the overall aesthetic integrity of the space. The result is a building that stands as a testament to architectural mastery, with every element working in harmony to create an inspiring environment.

title: The Elevated Acre
description:
Suspended high above the bustling streets of New York, The Elevated Acre is a testament to both design and structural ingenuity. This elevated public space offers sweeping views of the city while integrating steel and glass in a way that showcases the sophisticated interplay between transparency and support. Designed by Rogers Marvel, the structure features clean, transparent glass panels that reflect and enhance natural light, creating a unified radiance across the space. 
 
 Mariani Metal’s contribution to the project involved the fabrication and installation of the back beams that support the glass panels. These structural elements were crafted with precision to ensure that the design's minimalist aesthetic was not compromised, while also providing the necessary strength to support the weight of the elevated platform. 
 
 The project exemplifies Mariani’s ability to manage the delicate balance between steel and glass, ensuring both functionality and beauty. The Elevated Acre stands as a remarkable example of how Mariani’s expertise can bring complex architectural visions to life, combining artistry with engineering excellence.

title: Goldman Sachs
description:
The Goldman Sachs headquarters in New York City features one of the most iconic architectural elements in its grand lobby: a magnificent spiral staircase. This structure is a true reflection of Goldman Sachs’ esteemed reputation, combining advanced technology and artistry. Weighing 45 tons, the staircase was crafted from a complex mix of stone cladding, glass, and stainless steel, making it a centerpiece of both function and design. 
 
 Mariani Metal was integral to the staircase’s creation, taking on the highly detailed fabrication and assembly of this magnificent feature. The challenge was not only the design but also ensuring the flawless assembly of its intricate components. Every phase of the project was executed with the utmost precision, ensuring that no detail was overlooked. 
 
 A key part of Mariani’s approach was the creation of an exact-scale prototype in-shop. This allowed the team to explore numerous opportunities for welding efficiencies and refine the fabrication process to meet the project's exacting standards. As a result, 17 custom segments were fabricated and assembled with millimeter precision, creating a unified structure that seamlessly blended technological innovation with visual elegance. 
 
 The final product is a stunning work of architectural achievement. The staircase stands as both a functional piece and a visual triumph, elevating the aesthetic experience of the entire lobby. The successful execution of this project further solidified Mariani Metal’s standing as a leader in complex structural fabrication.

title: Mississauga Laser Centre
description:
The Mississauga Laser Centre is a striking example of architectural brilliance, where sharp angles and spiraling precision converge into an innovative design. Every element of the building showcases meticulous attention to detail, creating a sense of movement and energy throughout the structure. The design speaks to the centre’s commitment to cutting-edge technology and advanced medical treatments, while its bold architecture speaks volumes about its forward-thinking vision. 
 
 Mariani Metal played a critical role in bringing this vision to life, contributing to the fabrication of the building's complex structural components. The project demanded exacting precision and flawless craftsmanship, as each piece had to fit seamlessly into the intricate design conceived by Hariri Pontarini. 
 
 Mariani’s commitment to sustainability and refinement in both design and construction was integral to the project’s success. The company’s ability to execute such a complex design underpins its reputation for innovation and excellence in the fabrication industry. The result is a building that is not only visually stunning but also built to last, serving as a beacon of modern architecture in Mississauga.

title: Toronto Pearson Airport Terminal 1
description:
The Toronto Pearson Airport Terminal 1 stands as a landmark of modern airport design, combining functionality with cutting-edge aesthetics. This project posed an immense challenge due to its complex steel and glass construction, a design direction often considered too difficult due to the precise engineering required. However, this is where Mariani’s expertise in high-end architectural glazing came into play. 
 
 Mariani Metal’s role was integral in executing the sophisticated steel and glass elements that define the terminal’s iconic structure. The project involved the fabrication and installation of glass walls, exposed steel frameworks, glazing partitions, and pedestrian bridges, each requiring exceptional precision. The glass, used extensively across the terminal, enhances the building's openness and transparency, creating a welcoming environment for travelers. 
 
 Mariani’s team was able to overcome the inherent challenges of combining steel with glass, ensuring that each component was fabricated to exact specifications and installed with absolute precision. The use of exposed steel added an industrial elegance to the design, while the expansive glass elements allowed natural light to flood the terminal, enhancing its airy, open atmosphere. 
 
 The successful completion of Toronto Pearson Terminal 1 showcases Mariani’s unmatched ability to tackle intricate and ambitious architectural projects. The result is a terminal that not only serves as a major transportation hub but also as a testament to Mariani’s ingenuity, skill, and commitment to excellence in structural and architectural fabrication.

title: Luminous Veil
description:
The Luminous Veil is one of Toronto's most recognizable civic structures, a suicide prevention barrier installed in 2003 on the Prince Edward Viaduct, the historic Bloor Street bridge spanning the Don Valley. Designed by artist-architect Dereck Revington following a national competition, the Veil was never intended to be read as a barrier. It was conceived as a tensile landscape, a shimmering field of steel rods and cables that redefines the bridge deck as a contained urban space, trembling with light and movement against the valley below. 
 
 Mariani Metal fabricated the structural steel support system and the tensile rod-and-cable assembly that formed the Veil's core. Stretching 450 metres across both sides of the viaduct, the structure comprises over 9,000 stainless steel rods, each 12.7 centimetres apart and five metres high, tensioned between cantilevered girders and a horizontal support frame. The geometry demanded absolute symmetry across the full length of the bridge, a tolerance requirement that left no margin for error at scale. Fabricated at Mariani's Etobicoke facility, each component was engineered to perform structurally while disappearing visually into the skyline. 
 
 The result is a structure that functions as infrastructure and reads as art. Seen from the valley or the deck, the Luminous Veil does exactly what Revington intended, it holds the space with precision, and fills it with light.

title: NYU Gym
description:
The John A. Paulson Center at New York University is one of Manhattan's most ambitious academic and athletic facilities, 735,000 square feet across 23 floors, housing four NCAA-regulation basketball courts, a six-lane swimming pool, a varsity performance center, squash courts, and specialty training rooms for wrestling and fencing. Opened in 2023, the building replaced the former Coles Sports Center and became the permanent home of NYU Athletics. Built to LEED Gold standards, it is among the most complex mixed-use facilities constructed in New York City in recent years. 
 
 Mariani Metal contributed ornamental metalwork throughout the facility, fabricating and installing staircase systems, stainless steel tubular handrail systems, perforated metal wall cladding panels, and steel framed glazing partitions across the building's athletic corridors and circulation spaces. Each element was fabricated to specification at Mariani's Etobicoke facility and installed within one of the city's most technically demanding active construction environments. 
 
 At this scale, in this city, the tolerance for error is zero. That has always been Mariani's standard.

title: NYU Theatre
description:
The Iris Cantor Proscenium Theatre at NYU's John A. Paulson Center is the university's first professional-level performance venue, a 350-seat fly-loft theatre spread across three levels, designed to serve the Tisch School of the Arts and Steinhardt School of Music. Part of a $1.2 billion, 735,000 square foot facility opened in January 2023, the theatre represents NYU's most significant investment in performing arts infrastructure in its history. The space demanded a level of finish and architectural detail consistent with a world-class performance venue. 
 
 Mariani Metal fabricated and installed the custom laser-cut decorative steel panel system lining the theatre's interior, large-format black steel panels featuring an intricate organic pattern running continuously across the auditorium walls, balcony fascias, and stair enclosures across all three levels. The precision required to produce panels of this scale with a consistent laser-cut pattern, finished uniformly in black, and fitted seamlessly into a curved theatrical interior is considerable. Each panel had to perform acoustically, aesthetically, and structurally, meeting the demands of a live performance environment without compromise. 
 
 At Mariani, ornamental work at this scale is where craft becomes architecture.
